items.title: From typed text to integer cents
items.body:
A form input field always gives you text, even when it looks like a number. The guide's rule is: decide which texts are allowed (the *grammar*) before converting anything.

`parseCents` works in three steps:

1. A regular expression decides whether the text is an allowed decimal. Read it character by character and list some inputs it accepts and some it refuses (try spaces, signs, exponents, leading zeros, three decimals).
2. It splits the text at the dot and builds an integer number of cents from the whole part and the fraction padded to two digits ("5" becomes "50").
3. It checks the resulting number against a few bounds. Write down exactly which values pass.

The guide insists on integer cents rather than dollar amounts with fractions. Before reading its reason, open a console and add `0.1` to itself ten times, then compare with adding `10` ten times. When you read `renderTransactions`, look at how the totals are added up.

excerpts.quote: const [whole, fraction = ""] = text.split("."); const cents = Number(whole) * 100 + Number(fraction.padEnd(2, "0"));
Split whole and fractional text, right-pad the fraction and construct integer minor units. Do not multiply arbitrary fractional input and assume an exact result.

readMore.why: Validation versus normalization, applied to this data model.

items.title: Adding dollars as floats drifts; adding cents does not
items.body:
**Key: float error accumulates over many additions, while integer cents stay exact.**

Most decimal fractions, like 0.01 and 0.1, cannot be stored exactly in binary floating point; each is off by a tiny amount. With three rows the error is too small to show. With 100 additions of 0.01 the tiny errors add up, and the result can format to the wrong cent. `renderTransactions` avoids this by adding `Math.round(transaction.amount * 100)`, a whole number of cents, for each row, and dividing by 100 once at the end. Whole numbers add exactly. Exercise 2 asks for this 100 × 0.01 + 0.1 fixture so that the sum is $1.10 exactly.

Why the others are wrong:
- *formatCurrency truncates*: `Intl.NumberFormat` rounds; the drift happens earlier, in the sum.
- *reduce skips small amounts*: `reduce` visits every element.
- *MAX_SAFE_INTEGER after a hundred rows*: that limit is about 9 × 10^15, nowhere near.

excerpts.quote: summary[transaction.type] += Math.round(transaction.amount * 100);
**Accumulate cents, not dollars.** `total += transaction.amount` is fine for three rows and wrong for three hundred.

items.title: A stored zero amount can be read and deleted, not re-saved
items.body:
**Key: Save is refused with the positive-amount message, since parseCents rejects 0.**

Opening the editor copies the stored amount into the amount field, so it contains "0". On Save, `saveTransaction` runs `parseCents` on that field for edits too. "0" passes the regex, but the cents value is 0 and `cents > 0` fails, so it returns `NaN`. `transaction.amount` is then `NaN`, `Number.isFinite` is false, and the handler shows the "positive amount" message and returns without saving. The record stays as it was.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Only changed fields are re-validated*: the handler rebuilds and checks the whole transaction every time.
- *Bumped to 0.01*: nothing changes the amount; the save is refused.
- *Deleted*: the handler returns before `commitTransactions`, so nothing is written or removed.

excerpts.quote: return Number.isSafeInteger(cents) && cents > 0 && cents <= 99999999999 ? cents : NaN;
Open it in the editor, change its description, press Save, and you get the message about a positive amount. The record is readable and deletable, but not editable.

items.title: Why 'allow zero only when editing' is a trap
items.body:
**Key: validity would depend on how the user reached the form, which later surprises reusers.**

With `{ allowZero: editingId !== null }`, the same text "0" is valid money when you came from the Edit button and invalid when you came from the Add form. The rule about what money *is* now depends on navigation. The guide warns that this kind of rule is "correct for six months and then surprises everybody", including the next developer who calls `parseCents` from somewhere else and does not know about the flag.

Why the others are wrong:
- *editingId leaks into the next add*: `resetForm` sets `editingId = null`; the guide's objection is about the rule, not a leak.
- *Lets users create zero transactions via Add*: on Add, `editingId` is null, so `allowZero` is false.
- *An options object breaks the regex*: an extra argument does not change the regex test.

excerpts.quote: Now the validity of a value depends on *how you arrived at the form*, which is the kind of rule that is correct for six months and then surprises everybody - including the next developer who reuses `parseCents` somewhere a third way.

items.title: Save first, then show: the order of a commit
items.body:
Every create, edit and delete ends in `commitTransactions(next)`. `next` is the complete new list. The function writes it to localStorage and updates the in-memory `transactions` list that the screen is drawn from; when something goes wrong it shows "Could not save..." and returns `false`.

Two ideas from the concepts guide help you read this:

- **Order matters.** Changing memory and changing storage are two separate steps, and you have to choose which comes first. For each possible order, work out what the user would see if the storage write threw, and what they would see after reloading the page.
- **`try` and `await`.** The guide discusses what these two constructs do and do not give you when several separate storage calls are involved. Read that part and put its claim in your own words.

Before the quizzes, read `deleteTransaction` (lines 127-132) and `saveTransaction` and check what each does when `commitTransactions` returns `false`.

excerpts.quote: function commitTransactions(next) { try { localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(next)); }
Committing state is a separate boundary: serialize the full candidate, write it, then publish it.

readMore.why: How to state an invariant precisely enough to test it.

items.title: Number() accepts text that the money grammar refuses
items.body:
**Key: text like "1e3" or " 5 ", since Number takes them and the decimal regex never does.**

`Number("1e3")` is 1000 (scientific notation) and `Number(" 5 ")` is 5 (spaces are ignored). Both are positive, so `Math.round(Number(text) * 100)` with a `> 0` check accepts them. The current `parseCents` tests a strict regex first: digits, an optional dot and up to two digits, nothing else. "1e3" has a letter and " 5 " has spaces, so the regex fails and the function returns `NaN`. That is the guide's point: Number accepts forms that do not belong in a money field.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Only negatives*: `Math.round(-0.4 * 100)` is -40, which fails `> 0`.
- *Neither*: `Number` does not return NaN for those two inputs.
- *Only the empty string*: `Number("")` is 0, and the `> 0` check rejects 0.

excerpts.quote: Number inputs supply text. Define its grammar before conversion: Number accepts forms that do not belong in this currency workflow.

items.title: Why normalizeAmounts never writes back on load
items.body:
**Key: so a read never fails a write, and the next good commit persists the value.**

`normalizeAmounts` snaps old over-precise amounts to the cent as the data is loaded into memory. It deliberately does not call `setItem`. If loading also wrote to storage, then a user whose storage is full would get a failure just by opening the app; the guide says such a user "cannot open their budget at all". Instead the snapped values are saved by the next successful `commitTransactions`, which writes the whole list anyway.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Writing back would round again on each reload*: snapping an already-snapped value gives the same value, so repeated rounding is not the reason.
- *localStorage cannot be written during page load*: it can; the choice is deliberate.
- *Kept for rollback*: the comment gives only the read-never-fails-a-write reason, and the guide says rollback is not possible without keeping the original array.

excerpts.quote: Nothing is written back: the normalized value is persisted by // the next successful commitTransactions, so a read can never fail a write.
On load - which means a read can now fail a write, and a user with a full disk cannot open their budget at all

items.title: A filtered breakdown stops matching the whole-ledger totals
items.body:
**Key: a filtered breakdown stops adding up to the totals beside it unless scopes are labelled.**

`renderTransactions` computes `totals` with `transactions.reduce(...)`: the whole ledger. `visibleTransactions` (the filtered list) is only used to draw the rows. So `#income-total` ignores the filter and the search box. If a new category breakdown follows the filter, filtering to "income" gives a breakdown that no longer adds up to the totals next to it, and users will report it as a bug. Exercise 2 says to choose the scope deliberately and put it in the label.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Totals are hidden when filtering*: nothing hides them; they are always drawn.
- *Totals start following the filter too*: they use `transactions`, not `getVisibleTransactions()`.
- *Double-counting*: `getVisibleTransactions` returns each row at most once.

excerpts.quote: const visibleTransactions = getVisibleTransactions(); const totals = transactions.reduce((summary, transaction) => {
If your category totals follow the filter, then filtering to "income" makes the breakdown stop matching the totals beside it, and a user will report that as a bug.

items.title: Publish before saving and the change vanishes on reload
items.body:
**Key: the change would show on screen, then vanish on reload since storage lacked it.**

Today `commitTransactions` writes to localStorage first and assigns `transactions = next` only if the write did not throw. Swap them and memory changes first. If `setItem` then throws because storage is full, the `catch` shows a message and returns `false`, but `transactions` already holds the new list, so the screen can show the change. Storage still holds the old list, so after a reload the change is gone. The concepts guide describes exactly this order and its failure.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The browser retries the write*: localStorage has no queue or retry.
- *The catch restores the old array*: the catch only sets a message and returns `false`.
- *A failed setItem clears the key*: a failed write leaves the old stored value as it was.

excerpts.quote: try { localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(next)); } catch { setMessage("Could not save. Your transactions are unchanged; try again."); return false; } transactions = next;
If memory changes first and persistence fails, the UI can show data that will disappear after reload.

items.title: A migration needs to know which version it is reading
items.body:
**Key: it re-converts on each later load; store a schemaVersion and an explicit v1 to v2 step.**

"Multiply every amount by 100 on load" has no memory. On the first load, $12.50 becomes 1250 cents, correctly. On the next load the code cannot tell that 1250 is already in cents, so it multiplies again. The guide's fix is an envelope like `{ schemaVersion: 2, transactions: [...] }` and an explicit function that converts v1 to v2. Then a loader can see the version and convert only old data.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Negative expenses flip sign*: multiplying by 100 keeps the sign; expenses are told apart by `type`, not sign.
- *0.105 rounds down; use Math.ceil*: rounding is not the guide's problem here, and ceil would invent money.
- *Overflow of safe integers*: amounts up to 999,999,999.99 become about 10^11 cents, far below `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (about 9 × 10^15).

excerpts.quote: Store an envelope: `{ schemaVersion: 2, transactions: [...] }`, and write the conversion as an explicit `v1 → v2` function.

items.title: One try block around three calls is not a transaction
items.body:
**Key: try and await only route outcomes and do not make the calls atomic.**

*Atomic* means all of the steps happen or none of them do. If the second of three storage calls fails, the first has already happened, and a `try` block does not undo it; it only jumps to `catch`. `await` just waits for each call to finish or fail. To get atomicity you need a storage feature that provides it (a single write of the whole state, as `commitTransactions` does, or a real database transaction).

Why the others are wrong:
- *Atomic in browsers but not Node*: neither environment turns a `try` block into a transaction.
- *Fine if the catch rethrows*: rethrowing reports the error but does not undo earlier writes.
- *Atomic with Promise.all*: `Promise.all` runs calls together and rejects if one fails; the others may still have completed.

excerpts.quote: `await` does not make it infallible or atomic; it gives the caller a place to handle success and rejection. Similarly, calling several functions inside one `try` block does not create a database transaction.

items.title: Start here: a budget tracker that counts in cents
items.body:
This pack uses `budget-tracker`, a small browser app that records income and expenses in localStorage. The course is about three things: turning typed text into money safely, adding money without rounding errors, and saving to storage so the screen never shows something that was not saved.

Reading order, from the course README:

1. `budget-tracker/astraupskill/01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: where things are in `app.js`.
2. `02-CONCEPTS.md`: the ideas. Read the discussion of zero amounts closely.
3. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md` and `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md`.
4. `05-PRACTICE.md`: exercises 0-6. Several quizzes come from the traps these exercises describe.
5. `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md`, after trying them.

The code is all in `budget-tracker/app.js`. The functions to know are `parseCents` (lines 193-198), `commitTransactions` (205-210), `saveTransaction` (85-109), `renderTransactions` (150-191) and `normalizeAmounts` (71-79). Run `node --test test/money.test.cjs` to see the tests.

excerpts.quote: The central skill is **numeric parsing, representations and persisted state**.
node --test test/money.test.cjs

The map of app.js and the call path of one transaction.

items.title: Fixing zero records at the load boundary keeps one rule
items.body:
**Key: it keeps one input rule, since the impossible state is made impossible in the program.**

The guide's position 3 says: treat a zero-amount record as invalid data when it is loaded, the same way `normalizeAmounts` already handles over-precise amounts. The input rule (`parseCents` refuses zero) stays the same for every path, and once loading deals with zeros, no zero record can exist inside the running program. That avoids both a special edit-only rule and a record nobody can save.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Cheapest, loadTransactions already drops invalid records*: today nothing drops zero records on load; this is new work.
- *Lets the editor accept zero*: that is position 2, which the guide argues against.
- *No test needed*: the guide's lesson is to ask what a tightened validator does to existing data, which needs testing.

excerpts.quote: Treat a zero-amount record as invalid data on load, the same way `normalizeAmounts` (`app.js:71-83`) treats an over-precise one: quarantine it, or snap it to something, or refuse to display it. This keeps one rule for input *and* makes the impossible state impossible, which is usually the better trade.

items.title: The most important migration test: run it twice
items.body:
**Key: the v1 fixture run through the migration twice, since it must be idempotent.**

*Idempotent* means running something again gives the same result as running it once. A migration runs on every load, so it will see data it has already converted. The naive "multiply by 100" plan passes a single run but turns $12.50 into $1250.00 on the second, silently, for every user. Running a v1 fixture through the migration twice is the one test that catches that, which is why the test plan calls it the most important.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The v2 fixture*: it is in the plan, but it does not test repeated conversion.
- *The unconvertible record*: also in the plan, but the guide singles out the double run.
- *The plain v1 fixture*: one run proves the arithmetic, not that a second run is safe.

excerpts.quote: a v1 fixture run through the migration **twice** (the most important test - it must be idempotent), and one unconvertible record.
"Multiply every amount by 100 on load" is the naive plan and it double-converts on the second run, turning $12.50 into $1250.00

items.title: Why the failed-delete test compares raw strings
items.body:
**Key: a re-serialization with a new key order passes a deep compare but still rewrote storage.**

The promise is "a failed delete writes nothing". If the code rewrote storage with the same data, but with the object keys in a different order, then parsing both strings and deep-comparing the objects would say "equal", because key order does not matter to a deep compare. The stored text did change, though, so something was written. Only comparing the raw strings byte for byte proves that no write happened.

Why the others are wrong:
- *JSON.parse throws while setItem is stubbed*: the stub affects `setItem` only; reading and parsing still work.
- *Cross-realm deep compare fails*: the guide's reason is key order, not realms.
- *The raw string is faster*: speed is not the reason; strength of the check is.

excerpts.quote: the stored string is **byte-identical** (compare the strings, not re-parsed objects - a re-serialization with different key order would pass the weaker check);
if (!commitTransactions(transactions.filter((transaction) => transaction.id !== id))) return;

items.title: One parser should decide the reason, not two copies
items.body:
**Key: a second copy of the money rules in the handler would drift from the parser.**

If `saveTransaction` re-tested "too many decimals", "not a plain number" and so on, the rules about money would live in two places: `parseCents` and the handler. Sooner or later someone changes one (say, loosens the regex) and forgets the other, and the message no longer matches what the parser accepts. Exercise 1 says it "guarantees they will disagree within a month". If `parseCents` returns `{ error: "too-many-decimals" }`, one place decides what money is and the handler only turns the reason into a sentence.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The regex runs twice and is slow*: speed is not the guide's concern; a short regex is cheap.
- *Regexes block the event loop per keystroke*: validation runs on submit, and the issue is duplication.
- *Removes setMessage*: the handler still shows the message; it just maps the reason to text.

excerpts.quote: which gives you a second copy of the rules in `parseCents` (`app.js:193-198`) and guarantees they will disagree within a month - someone will loosen the regex and forget the handler.
Have `parseCents` return a reason (`{cents}` or `{error: "too-many-decimals"}`) so there is one place that decides.
